properties.title: HyperNSDE: Personalized Neural SDEs for Joint Static-Longitudinal Clinical Data Generation

properties.name: HyperNSDE joint static and longitudinal clinical-data generator
properties.membership: Verified learned clinical-time latent dynamics; level of independently evaluated successor prediction unresolved
properties.architecture: HI-VAE static mixed-type representation conditions a hypernetwork producing personalized deterministic ODE drift; separate population-shared stochastic residual Neural SDE. Deterministic latent state drives observation/EOS intensity. Both components start at zero and their separately decoded outputs are added.

properties.design: Synthetic fractional OU benchmarks with 30 newly generated datasets; retrospective VELOUR 526 patients and PPMI 1930 patients. Subject 80/20 split and 50 generated cohorts per fit; clinical results do not include 50 independent model refits.

assertions.rationale: Observation timestamps remain irregular, shifted to baseline and represented on their union grid; normalization does not assert measured result-availability times.
Continuous ODE/SDE evaluation at irregular times and explicit event process tested on generated/real grids, sparse visits and state-dependent monitoring.
Binary longitudinal mask distinguishes padded zero from observed entries; static ELBO includes observed entries only.

State-dependent point process plus EOS termination hazard generates visit patterns, assessed by empirical person-time intensity divergence and removal ablation. Actual intensity uses deterministic component.

80/20 original subject split and training-set longitudinal scaling are stated; exact fold-local variable selection, first observed baseline availability across channels and clinical temporal/site leakage audit not established.
criteria_met: Subject separation and training-only scale fit.
criteria_missing: Full preprocessing and feature-availability leakage audit.

assertions.rationale: HI-VAE converts static covariates and baseline measurements into discrete and continuous latents used by hypernetwork. No longitudinal encoder.
Observed static ELBO and longitudinal deterministic reconstruction MSE train encoder/dynamics; ablations assess reconstruction and downstream quality.
Static mixed-type/baseline covariates condition longitudinal dynamics through hypernetwork; joint losses connect static and longitudinal modalities without a longitudinal encoder.
Deterministic and stochastic latent states are carried across clinical-time integration steps and jointly decoded, initialized at zero with baseline levels represented statically.
Observed individual baseline values enter static latent and individual drift. No past longitudinal prefix encoder or recurrent factual reassimilation is implemented.
Same deterministic state feeds value decoder and variable/EOS intensity network; these are typed value versus observation-pattern readouts.
Clinical elapsed-time latent ODE and SDE map current latent states into later states and observations.
Neural deterministic drift hypernetwork, stochastic drift/diffusion and decoder are jointly trained on observed clinical trajectories. Generic SDE mathematics is not a physiological hybrid prior.
Population-shared Brownian Neural SDE residual generates nondegenerate path variation; deterministic-only ablation changes fidelity.
Integration advances internal latent states before value/intensity decoding.
Feed-forward decoder emits longitudinal deviations from deterministic and stochastic latents; generated recipe sums separately decoded components.
Observed-point reconstruction and signature-kernel path residual score optimize integrated paths across multiple clinical-time steps.
Generated paths integrate successive ODE/SDE states over full follow-up, without true intermediate replacement, then undergo sequence distribution comparisons.
Brownian residual sampling produces joint time-dependent paths conditional on static latent; 50 cohorts generated per fitted model.
No clearly matched target successor error for HyperNSDE. Clinical distribution comparisons assess cohort synthesis; reported TSTR forecasting uses separate S4 predictor.
S4 utility is not HyperNSDE successor error; cohort-level discrepancy does not by itself establish E1.
Conditional stochastic generative law defines path variability from shared Brownian residual; no claim of epistemic confidence or hidden-state posterior calibration.
Deterministic personalized trend and stochastic residual components are explicit; does not quantify epistemic versus aleatoric uncertainty or validate unique physiological separation.
criteria_met: Specified deterministic trend and stochastic residual decomposition.

assertions.rationale: Declared distance adversary uses generated cohort to discriminate training from held-out membership; MIR/NNAA computed and reported. Dep autocorrelation score is not individual memorization proof.
Membership adversary and nearest synthetic neighbor attack scores specified, but broader assets, access assumptions, state/planning interfaces and attack paths are not fully analyzed.
PDF explicitly names public HyperNSDE implementation repository and package; link not independently accessed.

50 generated cohorts per fit compared with held-out real joint distributions using longitudinal/static MMD, masked correlations, C2ST and intensity divergence. Evaluation is reported; this annotation does not establish a formal categorical acceptance outcome, so no pass/fail result is inferred.

Explicit synthetic binary subgroup, sparse-visit, limited-data and state-dependent-sampling tests; cohort-fidelity SMD. These do not constitute independent-site deployment testing. Evaluation is reported; this annotation does not establish a formal categorical acceptance outcome, so no pass/fail result is inferred.

Reference simulated training epoch approximately 80 seconds and total about 11 hours at epoch500 on single V10032GB/10CPUs; clinical timing scales but no universal runtime. Evaluation is reported; this annotation does not establish a formal categorical acceptance outcome, so no pass/fail result is inferred.

Predictive scoreWe assess downstream utility through a forecasting task under a Train-on-
Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol [17], compared with the Train-on-Real-Test-on-Real (TRTR)
baseline. A predictor based on an S4 architecture [19, 16], is trained to predict m future time points
(xi(tL+1:L+m)) from a observed prefix (xi(t1:L)) concatenated with static covariates. Missing values
are imputed via last-observation-carried-forward. Performance is measured using Mean Squared
Error (MSE) on real test data. Synthetic data yields better downstream utility when its TSTR MSE
closely matches the Train-on-Real (TRTR) reference.

Nearest-Neighbor Adversarial Accuracy (NNAA)NNAA [ 64] measures whether the synthetic
data distribution has systematically overfitted to the training data. For two datasets R (real) and S
(synthetic), the adversarial accuracy (AA) is defined as the proportion of samples that are closer to a
neighbor in their own set than to a neighbor in the opposite set:
AA(R, S) =12

where dAB(x) is the distance from x∈A to its nearest neighbor in B. If S simply memorizes R,
AA drops below 0.5. We compute this quantity once using the training set (AAtrain) and once using
a held-out test set ( AAtest). The final metric is NNAA = AA test −AA train. Large positive values
indicate that synthetic samples are systematically closer to training data than to unseen real data,
suggesting higher memorization risk. Distances are computed separately for static and longitudinal
modalities (using pairwise Euclidean and signature-based distances, respectively). For the multimodal
NNAA score, the modality-specific distance matrices are normalized and combined via a weighted
sum. Lower NNAA values indicate lower privacy risk.

evidence_fragments.content:
Membership Inference Risk (MIR)MIR [ 55] quantifies the vulnerability of the synthetic dataset
to a membership inference attack, assessing whether an adversary can distinguish training samples
from held-out test samples based strictly on their distance to the synthetic data. For each real sample
x, we compute an attack score s(x) =−d k(x, S), where dk is the aggregated distance (e.g., the
minimum or mean) to the k nearest synthetic neighbors. Treating training samples as the positive
class and test samples as the negative class, we evaluate the discriminative power ofs(x) using the
AUROC. We report the rescaled risk:
MIR = 2|AUROC−0.5|
so that MIR∈[0,1] , where 0 corresponds to random guessing (no privacy leak). As with NNAA,
MIR is computed per modality and then aggregated in the same manner. Lower MIR values indicate
lower privacy risk.

evidence_fragments.content:
Dependence ScoreWe report a dependence score based on the temporal autocorrelation structure.
For each longitudinal variable and lag k, we compute a dataset-level autocorrelation by averaging
patient-level Pearson autocorrelations over jointly observed pairs, yielding a matrix R∈R V×(K+1) .
The dependence score is the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the real and synthetic matrices:
Dep.Score = 1|Ω| X(v,k)∈Ω Rrealv,k −R synv,k 2
where Ω is the set of valid lag entries up to a maximum lag K. This metric serves as a critical dual-
purpose diagnostic. Primarily, it acts as a fidelity measure: generative models that over-smooth the
data fail to capture natural trajectory noise, resulting in an artificially high synthetic autocorrelation
and, consequently, a large MSE. Conversely, recent benchmarking by Stenger et al. [56] empirically
shows that autocorrelation error is also a top-performing proxy for privacy risk. If the error is
suspiciously close to zero, it indicates the model is likely memorizing the exact trajectory noise of
specific training samples rather than learning the underlying distribution. Thus, an optimal model
must achieve a low autocorrelation error without exactly replicating the training data.

evidence_fragments.content:
Several limitations remain. HyperNSDE learns the observational distribution of its training cohort
rather than causal counterfactuals, and therefore cannot by itself correct selection bias or extrapolate
to unsupported subgroups. It is also computationally more demanding than the baselines. More
broadly, our experiments show that existing metrics can disagree with trajectory realism for sparse,
irregular, stochastic data, while discriminative scores remain high for all methods, highlighting both
the difficulty of the problem and the limits of current approaches. In their present form, such models
may already support benchmarking use cases, but further progress is needed before they can be
confidently used for cohort augmentation or clinical trial simulation.
evidence_fragments.extractor_or_reviewer: Codex parallel source review; no independent human review

evidence_fragments.content:
These limitations suggest several directions for future work. On the modeling side, richer diffusion
parameterizations [44], including covariates-dependent diffusion terms, could improve the represen-
tation of subject-specific stochasticity. Extending the framework to typed longitudinal variables (e.g.,
integer, positive, or bounded) through adapted output distributions would also improve realism for
clinical biomarkers. Integrating differential privacy during training would provide formal guarantees
to complement our empirical privacy evaluation. On the methodological side, a deeper theoretical
and empirical study of the deterministic–stochastic decomposition would help clarify when and why
it improves training in sparse irregular settings. Finally, improving evaluation protocols and metrics
for synthetic irregular longitudinal data remains, in our view, the most important open problem, since
current metrics are still the main limiting factor for reliably assessing generated-data quality and for
making fair comparisons between models.

A.3 Extended details on synthetic data generation
As outlined in Figure 1, generating a fully synthetic individual follows a hierarchical sampling path.
This ensures that the generated longitudinal trajectories are intrinsically conditioned on the generated
static baseline characteristics. The exact procedure for generating a synthetic subject j is as follows:
1. Static covariate generation:We sample the latent representations hj = (s j,u j) from the
HI-V AE using eitherposteriororpriorsampling. Under posterior sampling, latent representations
are drawn from individual approximate posteriors q(si,u i |W i), then pooled, shuffled, and

sampling, they are drawn directly from the learned HI-V AE prior. We then decode these latents
to obtain the synthetic static covariates ˜Wj. The two sampling strategies are compared in the
sensitivity analysis Table 15.
2. Conditioning the dynamics:We map the static latent representation hj through the hypernetwork
H to generate the individualized drift parameters θb,j =H( ˜hj;θ H). This is the crucial step that
preserves the static–longitudinal dependency.
3. Latent trajectory simulation:In practice, rather than simulating the full latent SDE of Eq. (2) di-
rectly, we use the deterministic–stochastic decomposition introduced in Section 4 and simulate the
two components separately. The deterministic part zdetj (t) is obtained by solving the personalized
Neural ODE with individualized drift parameters θb,j, capturing the patient-specific smooth trend.
The stochastic residual zstoj (t) is simulated from the population-shared Neural SDE, capturing
intra-individual stochastic fluctuations. The full latent path is zj(t) =z detj (t) +zstoj (t), with both
components initialized at0 dz.
4. Irregular sampling simulation:To replicate the irregular observation patterns of the real data,
we compute the event intensities λj(t) based on the latent path via Equation (4), and sample a set
of discrete observation times ˜Tj.
5. Longitudinal decoding:Finally, we evaluate each latent component at the sampled observation
times and map these states through the decoder network to obtain the observable longitudinal
values: ˜xj(t) =g(z detj (t);θ g) +g(z stoj (t);θ g).
This yields synthetic multimodal records preserving static–longitudinal dependence, temporal vari-
ability, and irregular observation patterns.

evidence_fragments.content:
The signature-kernel MMD with an RBF static kernel, computed with PySigLib [54], depends
critically on the bandwidth parameter σ. If σ is poorly matched to the scale of pairwise path
discrepancies in signature space, the kernel values saturate, and the metric loses discriminative power.
In this regime, the empirical estimator may also become numerically unstable; in particular, the
unbiased estimate of MMD2 can take negative values at finite sample size, and this effect may be
exacerbated in practice by long, sparse, and highly irregular trajectories. To improve stability, we
select σ using a median heuristic applied after time augmentation and path compression, and we
linearly interpolate trajectories between observed points before computing the signature kernel. The
latter ensures that the evaluated paths are piecewise linear, but sparse and irregular sampling may still
make the interpolated paths only rough proxies for the underlying continuous trajectories. As a result,
the signature-kernel MMD should be interpreted with caution, especially when comparing models
that differ substantially in smoothness or in the induced observation patterns.

Discriminative scoreAs a joint fidelity measure, we use a classifier two-sample test (C2ST) [ 66]:
a classifier is trained to distinguish real from synthetic samples, taking as input the longitudinal
trajectories (with last-observation-carried-forward imputation) augmented with static covariates. The
classifier is based on an S4 architecture [19] with masked global average pooling, ensuring predictions
depend only on observed time steps. We report the test AUROC; values closer to 0.5 indicate that
synthetic samples are harder to distinguish from real data, and hence better fidelity.

evidence_fragments.content:
All models are trained using AdamW [37]. HyperNSDE is trained with early stopping (patience 10,
maximum 1000 epochs). All experiments were run on the Jean Zay cluster using single-GPU jobs on
NVIDIA V100 GPU with 32 GB of memory, 10 CPU cores per task. and a wall-clock limit of 20
hours per job. On the reference simulated dataset, one epoch takes approximately 1 min 20 s, with
training terminating around epoch 500 (≈11 hours). Training time scales with the number of patients
and observations for real-world datasets.

evidence_fragments.content:
F.4 Subgroup and cohort analyses
We complement the aggregate evaluation with analyses of subgroup-specific fidelity on simulated
data and source-cohort representativeness on VELOUR.
HyperNSDE learns the observational distribution represented in its training cohort. To assess how
closely the generated population reproduces the source cohort, we compare real and synthetic static
covariates on VELOUR using standardized mean differences (SMDs). Across the 26 static covariates,
the median SMD is 0.092, indicating close agreement with the observed VELOUR cohort. This
assesses fidelity to the source population and should not be interpreted as a correction of selection
bias or representativeness with respect to a broader target population.

capability_assessments.rationale: The three core identity conditions are implemented over clinical time, with baseline-conditioned free-running latent trajectories and distributional evaluation. However, TSTR future MSE evaluates a separately trained S4 predictor, not HyperNSDE successor predictions. No direct time-indexed future-state target error or matched conditional forecasting protocol is established for HyperNSDE. Retain verified core membership and E3, without automatically assigning L0 or L1.

limitations: Clinical datasets are independently fit domains, not external held-out deployment transfer; 50 generated cohorts do not measure model refit variability.
No prospective care study, action-conditioned causal effect identification or model-coupled planner. VELOUR trial provenance does not make this generator a randomized treatment-effect evaluation.
TSTR MSE belongs to a separate S4 model and does not validate generator conditional future prediction.
Clinical C2ST AUROC 0.998 VELOUR and 0.996 PPMI means generated patients remain easily distinguishable. Strong selected MMD results do not establish clinical realism.
Posterior sampling pools approximate static posteriors; patient correspondence is discarded, but that alone is not a privacy mechanism. No differential privacy guarantee.
Code release and restricted data access are stated in PDF, not externally verified.
Single Codex source review; no independent human review, external source retrieval, code execution/replication or prospective clinical validation performed by reviewer.
All main-PDF pages including references/appendices read; every identified figure/table inspected. Referenced studies are bibliography only and do not transfer capabilities.
Mechanical schema/source/coverage checks establish necessary conditions and quote occurrence, not scientific truth or clinical safety.
